TDM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
OBJECTIVES
w Determine if a TDM transmitter and receiver system is operating correctly.
w Identify the faulted component in a malfunctioning TDM transmitter and receiver system.
. The experiment in this lesson is not setup to use the selected trainer.
EQUIPMENT REQUIRED
Definition
Definition
In this lesson, you will troubleshoot faults in a TDM transmitter and receiver system.
INTRODUCTIONM
The same process that is used to troubleshoot modulating signal processing systems is used to troubleshoot multiplexing signal processing systems.
In fact, all transmitter and receiver systems use the same method.
You find out if the receiver's output signal is correct. If not, you locate the fault to the transmitter or receiver.
Let's begin the lesson on TDM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING.....................

TDM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
In this experiment, you will locate the failed chip or component in a TDM transmitter and receiver system.
EXPERIMENT
Definition
The transmitter consists of the components necessary to time multiplex information signals.
PC130-305 SCHEMATIC - Transmitter
The receiver consists of the components necessary to demultiplex TDM signals.
To locate a faulted chip or support component, you must first determine if the TDM system is operating correctly.
To do this, you check each input signal to the transmitter against each output signal of the receiver.
If one or more of the output signals are incorrect, then the system is faulted.
If the system is faulted, you determine if the transmitter or receiver is causing the problem.
If the output of the transmitter is bad, the multiplexer circuits are faulted.
If the output of the transmitter is good, the fault is in the transmission medium or receiver.
If the input to the receiver is bad, the fault is in the transmission medium.
If the input to the receiver is good, the demultiplexer circuits are faulted.

Once the fault has been located, further oscilloscope or multimeter measurements will locate the fault to a particular chip or component. Remember, use an analog multimeter to check out a transistor. Let's start the experiment.

The output signal on TP9 of the multiplexer is correct for the sync pulse and three of the four information signals. The multiplexer is not faulted.
TRY AGAIN!
The output signal on TP9 of the multiplexer is correct for the sync pulse and three of the four information signals. The control/clock circuits are not faulted.
Which IC or component is most likely to cause the fault?
The input to IC1 on pin 5 for channel 2 is zero. The op-amp can not operate with an incorrect input.
TRY AGAIN!
The signal is not present to the input of C4. Look for the signal at the input of the amplifier.
Congratulations, you determined that the fault is C3 grounded.
The computer will now remove the fault. Check the output of the receiver on the PC130-306 channel TPs and verify the TDM system is operating correctly.
